title: Facing conflict early and staying objective
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Team leaders who mediate disputes within the crew or between the crew and others on a site.
learningOutcomes: Name a conflict early and set out the facts before proposing a solution.
Mediate between two crew members without taking sides.
Choose which fights to take on and which to leave, using the resources available.

instruction.heading: Name the conflict early
instruction.body: Many leads hope a conflict will fade. It usually grows. Naming a disagreement calmly, while it is still small, gives the people involved a chance to resolve it. The aim is not to win but to acknowledge that a problem exists and to work on it. Differences of opinion about method can be useful when they are aired openly, because they often reveal a better way of doing the job.

instruction.heading: Mediating without taking sides
instruction.body: When you mediate, hear each person separately, then together. Keep your own view out of it unless you are asked for it. Look for the shared interest, such as getting the job done to standard before the client returns. If the other party is not a crew member but a client or another contractor, define the limits of what you can agree on and what needs the supervisor's decision. A mediator who appears to favour one side loses the crew's trust quickly.

instruction.heading: Choosing battles and working with others
instruction.body: Not every disagreement is worth a formal process. Consider how much the issue matters, how much support you have, and whether you can win without damaging the crew. Look for collaboration within the crew and with other teams that share the same aim. Where a proposed arrangement conflicts with the business's standards, do not agree to it just to end the dispute.

procedure: Note the disagreement, the people involved and the date it was first noticed.
Speak to each person privately and listen to their account without interrupting.
Bring the two people together and restate each account neutrally.
Identify a shared goal and agree one practical step each person will take.
Set a check date and confirm the step has been taken.
Refer to the supervisor any part of the dispute that is outside your authority.

workedExamples.situation: Two workers on a bond clean disagree about whether the oven clean was included in the agreed scope, and the dispute is getting heated in front of the agent.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How should the lead step in, and what must be checked before deciding?
workedExamples.reasoning: The lead moves the discussion away from the agent, hears each worker separately, checks the job sheet and the agreed scope, and then restates the facts neutrally. The shared goal is an accurate job record. If the scope is unclear, the lead refers the question to the supervisor rather than deciding it alone.

equipmentAndPpe: Job sheet and agreed scope document. Standard PPE on site.

commonErrors.error: Waiting for the conflict to resolve itself.
commonErrors.prevention: Raise a disagreement the moment it surfaces.

commonErrors.error: Taking the side of the more senior or more popular worker.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the written record to test each account.

commonErrors.error: Making a decision about scope or pricing that belongs to the supervisor.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the decision boundary and refer what is outside your authority.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Conflict that involves a safety concern must be treated as a safety matter first.

qualityStandard: The mediation record shows the facts from each person and the neutral restatement.
The agreed step is specific, has an owner and a check date.
documentationEvidence: Dispute record with dates, people and facts.
summary: Name conflict while it is small.
Mediate by listening to each side, restating the facts neutrally and finding a shared goal.
Refer scope, pricing and safety matters that are outside your authority.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a lead name a disagreement early?
options: Because a small disagreement is easier to resolve before it grows
Because early conflict usually means the worker has made a mistake
Because the client must be told immediately
Because the supervisor requires a report for every disagreement

knowledgeChecks.question: What does an objective mediator do?
options: Supports the person with more seniority and hears the other side only briefly
Listens to each side, restates the facts neutrally and keeps their own view out of it
Decides the outcome without hearing both people and tells both sides what to do
Avoids the discussion until the job is finished and then tells both people to forget it

knowledgeChecks.question: A dispute involves a pricing change. What should the lead do?
options: Agree a price to end the dispute on the spot with the crew and the client
Ask the crew to vote on the price and then agree the result with the client
Refer the pricing question to the supervisor because it is outside the lead's authority
Settle the pricing with the client, then focus on the cleaning and tell the supervisor afterwards

knowledgeChecks.question: According to the lesson, is every disagreement worth a formal process?
options: Yes, every disagreement needs a formal process
No. Not every disagreement is worth a formal process
